transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Markus Chen (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Redwood Solutions), Tom Weaver (Redwood SRE), David Park (CascadeHR CTO), Priya Singh (CascadeHR Platform Eng), Rafael Gomez (CascadeHR ML Infra), Maya Li (CascadeHR Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Redwood team walked through session-store/KV eviction behavior under heavy prefix reuse and long-context sessions. Discussed prefetch heuristics, paging to local NVMe, batching impact on latency SLOs, and constraints for VPC/on-prem deployments. Action items: run bench, share security docs, confirm network.

Transcript:
[00:00:03] Lena Ortiz: All right everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna focus today on CascadeHR's session-store patterns — eviction, paging, and some prefetch ideas. Markus and Tom from our runtime team are on deck.
[00:00:18] David Park: Great, thanks Lena. We've been seeing tail latency spikes and some token regressions when users hit long sessions — hiring workflows can go 8-10k tokens.
[00:00:29] Markus Chen: Right. To frame it: Redwood's session store (we often call it the KV layer internally) holds per-token KV caches keyed by prefix id. Under memory pressure we evict least-recently-used prefix segments but there are subtle hotspots when many sessions share similar prefixes.
[00:00:45] Priya Singh: By similar prefixes you mean like shared system prompts or templates? That's exactly our case — 70% of sessions reuse the company's interview template.
[00:00:53] Markus Chen: Exactly. That creates prefix reuse hotspots which compress effective working set but also increases collision probability in the in-memory slab allocator.
[00:01:06] Rafael Gomez: Can you expand on "collision probability" — is that KV key collisions or memory allocator fragmentation?
[00:01:12] Markus Chen: Mostly allocator fragmentation + logical prefix shadowing. We track entries by (session_id, prefix_id, token_index) but runtime prefetch groups contiguous token ranges. When many sessions access identical prefix_id, our cache indexing still stores separate KV segments per session which increases metadata pressure.
[00:01:29] Tom Weaver: Also worth noting eviction is per-GPU shard; in Dedicated or Private each worker has its own cache and we use a distributed LRU-ish coordination for spillback decisions. If shard A evicts, we may page to NVMe or request the prefix from Redis-like backing store depending on config.
[00:01:49] Maya Li: On the security side we need to understand what gets written to disk when paging happens. Is that encrypted? Where are KMS keys used?
[00:01:57] Aisha Patel: Short answer: when paging to local NVMe in Private deployments, we provide an encrypted page file; keys can be customer-managed via KMS/HSM. We also support not paging to disk (in-memory only) if you enforce that policy. We'll send the SOC2 + KMS integration docs after.
[00:02:12] Priya Singh: Good. Back to behavior — our retention TTLs vary: we keep session context for 24 hours, but some orchestrations reattach contexts weeks later which spikes retrievals.
[00:02:23] Markus Chen: That's a classic TTL drift problem. Two things happen: 1) metadata (prefix pointers) remain, but the actual dense KV blobs are evicted; 2) when reattach happens there's a cold read storm and prefetch heuristics may under-provision for the simultaneous rehydrates.
[00:02:39] David Park: We observed 'burst restore' where latency jumps for first 200-300 tokens and then stabilizes.
[00:02:45] Markus Chen: That matches a paging + k-v fetch waterfall. Our runtime can prefetch subsequent token blocks asynchronously, but we tune heuristics by typical session length distribution. For example, for long contexts we can proactively warm the last N prefixes.
[00:02:58] Rafael Gomez: What about batching? We're trying to maximize throughput for nightly candidate scoring jobs but not blow up latency for interactive UI calls.
[00:03:06] Tom Weaver: Batching trades latency for tokens-per-second efficiency. We expose separate routes: interactive path with strict SLO (small batch windows, aggressive priority) and batch path with larger batch windows. For mixed workloads we recommend dedicated pools or strict traffic shaping.
[00:03:19] Priya Singh: Can Redwood do dynamic prioritization between interactive and batch at the router level?
[00:03:24] Markus Chen: Yes — smart routing can steer by header flags. You can tag requests as 'low-priority/batch' and they will be queued into batch pools; interactive tagged requests get preemptive slots. That avoids prefix eviction oscillation from batch floods.
[00:03:36] David Park: We also want to try 4-bit quantized models to save memory. How does quantization affect KV storage?
[00:03:43] Markus Chen: Quantization primarily reduces model weights in GPU memory; KV caches (the attention key/value activations) are still floating activation tensors, so size reductions there come from shorter sequence lengths, compression, or lossy quantization of cached activations — which we don't generally enable by default because of quality regressions. We have experimental activation compression (8->6-bit heuristics) but it's per-customer opt-in.
[00:04:05] Maya Li: Anything we should be aware of for on-prem NVMe paging and compliance?
[00:04:09] Aisha Patel: We can do ephemeral encryption with customer KMS; audit logs record page write/read events. We provide a manifest of what metadata is persisted. If your policy forbids paging, there's a toggle to disable spill-to-disk entirely.
[00:04:22] Priya Singh: Nice. For our tests can we change eviction thresholds at runtime? We don't want to redeploy to tweak heuristics.
[00:04:28] Tom Weaver: Yes, in Private/Dedicated you can set runtime knobs via the Console or config API: target_resident_kv_bytes, per-prefix_ttw (time-to-warm), and prefetch_window tokens. These take effect without full restart.
[00:04:39] David Park: Walk us through a recommended setup for heavy prefix reuse + long-context interactive sessions.
[00:04:44] Markus Chen: Recommendation: 1) Increase per-shard resident_kv_bytes to hold hot prefixes; 2) Enable prefix coalescing (we'll explain) — this merges identical prefix payloads into a shared read-only store when you opt in; 3) Tune prefetch_window to 128-256 tokens for interview flows; 4) Use dedicated pool for interactive so batch jobs don't evict.
[00:05:02] Rafael Gomez: Can you expand on prefix coalescing? Sounds promising.
[00:05:07] Markus Chen: Sure. With coalescing we canonicalize prefix_id content and store a single immutable KV for the canonical prefix, then session metadata points to that shared block. It reduces memory duplication for template-heavy workloads. Caveat: coalescing requires that your application treats shared prefix blobs as read-only — if you mutate session-specific tokens into that block it breaks isolation.
[00:05:27] Priya Singh: We do sometimes insert ephemeral per-session markers into templates. Is there a hybrid approach?
[00:05:32] Markus Chen: Yes — split your prompt into a static canonical prefix and a small dynamic suffix. Coalesce the static part and keep the suffix in per-session KV. That preserves memory savings while maintaining per-session mutability.
[00:05:42] Maya Li: How do we debug when we see eviction hot loops? We've seen repeated evict/rehydrate cycles for the same prefixes.
[00:05:50] Tom Weaver: Our recommended telemetry: enable per-prefix hit counters, eviction reasons (age vs memory-pressure vs manual TTL), and a tail-latency histogram. We'll give you an alpha dashboard. Look for patterns: if evictions are caused by a small set of large prefixes, coalescing or increasing resident_kv can help; if evictions are due to bursts, consider throttling or reserving burst capacity.
[00:06:10] Lena Ortiz: We have a short demo of a prefetch heuristic tweak and traces — Markus?
[00:06:15] Markus Chen: (shares screen) Ok, here's a trace from a live sim. At 00:00:00 you see a cold start; our async prefetch kicks in on token 4 and warms tokens 5-64. On this run, prefetch window was 64 tokens and we see steady latencies after token 30. 
[00:06:32] [screen audio: noises]
[00:06:38] Markus Chen: If we increase prefetch to 256 we pay more memory but reduce early-token tail. In tests we measured p95 reduce from 450ms to 180ms for long sessions, but resident_kv_bytes went up by ~30%.
[00:06:52] Priya Singh: That's a useful trade-off. Our SLO is p95 < 250ms for interactive — seems prefetch 256 hits it.
[00:06:59] Rafael Gomez: Are there scenarios where prefetch harms throughput for batch?
[00:07:03] Tom Weaver: Yes — if you over-aggressively prefetch for every batch job, you fill caches with transient prefixes and evict hot interactive data. That's why we advise separate routing or prefetch policies per route.
[00:07:15] David Park: About TLS and VPC — we plan to use Private deployment in our GCP region and peer with our VPC. Any pitfalls?
[00:07:22] Aisha Patel: Recommend validating MTU, egress NAT for GPUs, and routing to private endpoints. Also confirm that your peering allows high-throughput RPCs — we use gRPC with streaming; suboptimal MTU can increase packetization overhead for KV transfer.
[00:07:36] Priya Singh: Regarding logs, we need per-token cost breakdown since finance asks for per-flow chargeback.
[00:07:42] Lena Ortiz: Console can export token-level cost telemetry segmented by model, route, and prefix_tag. We'll include an example CSV.
[00:07:48] Maya Li: Back to compliance: if we enable NVMe paging but need logs stripped of PII, can Redwood scrub before writing pages?
[00:07:56] Markus Chen: We can provide hooks to run an application-level scrubber prior to writing; however, scrubbing before paging adds compute overhead and potential latency. If PII must never leave RAM, disable spill-to-disk.
[00:08:09] David Park: For our initial pilot what's the minimal config to avoid cold storms?
[00:08:14] Markus Chen: Minimal: set resident_kv_bytes to 2x your observed working set, enable async prefetch at 128 tokens, route interactive to a small Dedicated pool, and set ephemeral TTL to 7 days for the pilot. Then run the 24h prefix-heavy stress test.
[00:08:28] Priya Singh: Let's talk troubleshooting steps when we do see a cold-storm event.
[00:08:33] Tom Weaver: Step 1: capture the per-shard eviction log and the top-50 prefix eviction reasons. Step 2: correlate with ingress timestamps to see if it's a reattach event storm. Step 3: if it's prefix duplication, enable coalescing. Step 4: if it's batch interference, route batch to separate pool. Step 5: when unclear, send full bundle to Redwood support with logs and we'll triage.
[00:08:56] Rafael Gomez: Great. If we opt into activation compression, any warning signs to watch?
[00:09:00] Markus Chen: Watch for hallucination rate increases on sensitive prompts and slight shifts in token probabilities. We'll run A/B evals and show delta metrics. It's opt-in and you can pin rollbacks in the Console.
[00:09:11] David Park: Ok. A few quick Qs from Rafael on prefix shadowing.
[00:09:15] Rafael Gomez: Is there an API to snapshot prefix maps for audit?
[00:09:18] Tom Weaver: Yes, a read-only manifest API that lists prefix IDs, canonical flags, resident bytes, and last-touch timestamps. We'll give you scoped credentials to query that.
[00:09:28] Priya Singh: Could we prototype coalescing in a staging cluster?
[00:09:31] Lena Ortiz: Absolutely — Markus will run a coalescing simulation in our staging and provide a diff of memory use.
[00:09:38] Markus Chen: I'll seed the sim with CascadeHR's template distribution if you provide anonymized sample prompts. We only need shape, not PII.
[00:09:46] David Park: We'll provide a sanitized sample.
[00:09:49] Priya Singh: One last thing: can Redwood surface when a prefix is shared vs private so our app telemetry can tag flows?
[00:09:56] Markus Chen: Yes, we'll add a boolean 'coalesced' tag in the telemetry export so you can filter flows and measure impact.
[00:10:03] Lena Ortiz: Ok wrapping up — quick recap and next steps.
[00:10:07] Lena Ortiz: Markus to run the 24h prefix-heavy benchmark and share logs; we'll demo coalescing sim in staging; Lena to send SOC2 + KMS doc; Priya to share VPC screenshots. Follow-up in two weeks.
[00:10:20] David Park: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[00:10:23] [call continues with casual sign-off and short side chatter]
